title: Signal · Saturday 31 October
overview: Euro area supervisors put generative AI use at about 85 percent of banks, Bern finds a UBS move abroad would bring little capital relief, and North Korean hackers are blamed for a record theft from Binance.
status_line: Complete edition: Friday's briefing could read only 3 of 49 sources, so this one also brings the Thursday and Friday stories it missed.

top.headline: ECB supervisor puts generative AI use at about 85 percent of banks
top.summary: Pedro Machado, a member of the ECB's Supervisory Board, said in a Bloomberg interview the ECB published on 30 October that around 85 percent of banks already use generative AI, from fraud detection and KYC to credit scoring. He warned that frontier AI models shorten the time between a vulnerability being found and exploited, which makes fast patching banks' biggest challenge. The same day, Executive Board member Philip Lane said the AI boom adds about 0.9 percentage points to euro area credit growth, around a quarter of the total.
top.background: In July the ECB asked significant banks for action plans on AI-enabled cyber threats by 31 October; Machado said a fuller assessment will follow once they are in.
top.why: Security and AI governance leads at significant euro area banks should expect supervisory follow-up and comparison of their plans across banks.

top.headline: Swiss finance ministry finds a UBS move abroad would bring little capital relief
top.summary: An internal assessment by the Federal Department of Finance, reported by Reuters on 29 October, found that UBS would gain little by moving to the US or the UK to escape tougher Swiss capital rules. US holding-company rules would tie up about as much capital as the Swiss proposal, and in the UK the Swiss business would carry much heavier risk weights. The ministry called the Federal Council's proposal effective, targeted, proportionate and manageable for UBS.
top.background: Reuters puts the possible extra CET1 need at about $18 billion; the Council of States voted in September for 90 percent backing of foreign units instead of 100.
top.why: Lawmakers now have the government's own view that relocating would spare UBS little capital, as the National Council takes up the rules.
top.watch_next: The National Council committee's debate in November, ahead of a possible vote in December.

top.headline: North Korean hackers blamed for a record $6.3 billion theft from Binance
top.summary: An attacker moved about $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains on the evening of 29 October, most of it within about 20 minutes, according to TRM Labs, which attributes the theft with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored group; Chainalysis agrees. Binance first pointed to a compromised engineer's laptop with access to a service used to submit withdrawals, later found further points of breach, and has set aside over $6.34 billion of its own funds to cover losses.
top.background: Around $3 billion has been frozen with partners, Binance says. TRM calls it the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the Bybit hack of February 2025.
top.why: Banks and Swiss custodians running digital asset desks will be asked how their hot-wallet signing and engineers' devices would stand up to the same playbook.
top.watch_next: Whether withdrawals resume on schedule this weekend.

items.headline: Swiss Bankers Association wants banks to issue franc stablecoins under their licences
items.summary: In a paper presented in Zurich on 29 October, the Swiss Bankers Association said a Swiss franc stablecoin should be issued from Switzerland under FINMA supervision. It wants banks to issue stablecoins under their existing banking licence, rather than through the separate subsidiary the Federal Council's draft revision of the Financial Institutions Act requires, and more flexible reserve rules.
items.why: Banks testing a franc stablecoin in a sandbox since September, among them UBS, PostFinance, Raiffeisen and Zürcher Kantonalbank, would be spared a separately licensed subsidiary if parliament agrees.

items.headline: Swiss private bank Piguet Galland reports about 10 percent efficiency gains from Copilot
items.summary: Jordi Domenech, head of technology at Piguet Galland, told WealthBriefing on 29 October that the bank of about 180 staff rolled out Microsoft Copilot after investing in cloud infrastructure, document classification and training, and reports efficiency gains of around 10 percent. It now also runs large language models on its own infrastructure for internal uses such as help desks, and keeps AI away from clients for now.
items.why: A small Swiss private bank getting measurable gains from standard tools and self-hosted models sets a pattern peers of its size can follow.

items.headline: Zurich legal insurer Dextra puts iudexnc's AI coverage checks into regular use
items.summary: Dextra, a Zurich legal expenses insurer handling about 40,000 cases a year, now uses start-up iudexnc's software in regular operations to check whether claims are covered, after a pilot that began in October 2025, startupticker.ch reported. The AI proposes a coverage decision citing the relevant policy clauses and a specialist decides; in the last pilot measurement it matched specialists 90 percent of the time.
items.why: A human-in-the-loop claims deployment with a published agreement rate is the kind of evidence Swiss insurers' risk and compliance teams ask for before scaling AI.

items.headline: ING says agentic AI cut complex mortgage approvals from seven days to five
items.summary: ING chief executive Steven van Rijswijk said on the third-quarter call on 29 October that agentic AI in Dutch mortgages has cut the approval time for complex mortgages from seven days to five, and that ING plans to extend it to other markets. The bank's net result rose 3.5 percent to €1,850m, and a Wholesale Banking restructuring will bring around 400 redundancies.
items.why: A measured cut in approval time from an agentic process is the kind of benchmark European retail banks will be asked for in their own AI business cases.

items.headline: ECB picks two consortia to connect banks to the digital euro
items.summary: The ECB has chosen a Nexi and Deutsche Telekom consortium and a Telefónica and Minsait consortium as the digital euro's two network service providers, each on a ten-year contract, according to The Paypers and the companies. The networks will give banks, payment providers and national central banks secure access to the platform; from 2029, if the digital euro is issued, banks can connect through either.
items.why: Euro area banks and payment providers planning digital euro integration now know which two networks they will have to connect to and test against.

items.headline: SNB reports a CHF 44.2 billion profit for the first nine months
items.summary: The Swiss National Bank reported a profit of CHF 44.2 billion for the first three quarters of 2026. Foreign currency positions earned CHF 43.3 billion, gold added CHF 1.2 billion and Swiss franc positions CHF 0.1 billion; the SNB said only provisional conclusions are possible for the full year, and the allocation to currency reserve provisions is set at year-end.
items.why: Federal and cantonal finance departments planning 2027 watch this figure, since any SNB distribution depends on the year-end result.

items.headline: Luzerner Kantonalbank lifts nine-month profit 8.7 percent on fee and trading growth
items.summary: Luzerner Kantonalbank's group profit rose 8.7 percent to CHF 242.7 million in the first nine months of 2026, on operating income up 7.7 percent to CHF 555.8 million. Commission income grew 12.8 percent and trading 13.0 percent, against 4.3 percent for net interest income; the bank expects 2026 profit in the upper third of its CHF 305 to 320 million range.
items.why: A benchmark for cantonal banks: mandate volumes reached CHF 18.534 billion, from CHF 16.842 billion at the end of 2025, as fees carry profit growth.

items.headline: Lagarde will step down as ECB President on 7 February 2027
items.summary: Christine Lagarde has told the ECB Governing Council and European Council President António Costa that she will step down as ECB President on 7 February 2027, the ECB said on 29 October; the European Council will appoint her successor. The ECB gave no reason. Fidelity International's Conor Parle named Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot as frontrunners, according to WealthBriefing.
items.why: A succession race through early 2027 adds uncertainty to the euro rate path, which feeds into European bank margins and the franc.

items.headline: NatWest shares slide as it guides to a broadly flat margin into 2027
items.summary: NatWest's third-quarter attributable profit fell 4.1 percent to £1,532m on income up 7.1 percent to £4,640m, according to its filing on 30 October. Reuters reported the shares fell 8.4 percent after management guided to a net interest margin broadly stable at 2.5 percent into 2027, below expectations. The filing says an AI fraud-triage agent is now live for credit card customers.
items.why: With margins flat, UK banks' AI and wealth spending will be judged on savings and fee income; NatWest cites about £420m of gross cost savings.

items.headline: CD&R and GTCR explore taking payments processor Global Payments private
items.summary: Clayton, Dubilier & Rice is exploring a take-private of Global Payments together with GTCR, its largest shareholder, according to the Financial Times and Reuters on 30 October. The FT put the enterprise value at around $40 billion, which would rank among the largest buyouts on record; the shares rose more than 11 percent. The talks are at an early stage, and the firms declined to comment.
items.why: Banks that partner with Global Payments or Worldpay on merchant acquiring could end up dealing with a heavily indebted private owner focused on cost and pricing.

items.headline: Mistral releases open weights for Large 4, its trillion-parameter model
items.summary: Mistral released the weights of Mistral Large 4 on 29 October, a natively multimodal model with 1 trillion parameters trained from scratch on European infrastructure, after a public preview earlier in October. Mistral calls it the best open-weight model for coding; it offers low, medium and high reasoning modes, and the weights are on Hugging Face as well as Mistral's API.
items.why: Banks that cannot send data to US clouds now have a trillion-parameter open model they can run and audit in their own data centres, security work included.
items.for_your_skills: For your skills: Architecture & TOM can now cite a European-trained, open-weight model of this size for on-premises or Swiss-hosted designs, with three reasoning modes to balance cost.

items.headline: China-linked hackers ran an AI agent framework against more than 200 organisations
items.summary: CrowdStrike says the China-based group it tracks as Vapor Panda used ARTEX, an AI-driven intrusion framework running on DeepSeek and possibly a second commercial model, against more than 200 organisations in at least 14 countries from 17 October, finance entities among them. Planner and worker agents ran several intrusions at once, with a human operator steering at decision points; CrowdStrike confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organisations.
items.why: Bank security teams should plan for intrusions run in parallel at machine pace, which shortens the time to catch misuse of leaked or unrotated credentials.

items.headline: Nine AI developer platforms breached in October as stolen AI keys are resold
items.summary: Wiz researchers counted at least nine AI developer platforms that disclosed incidents in October, among them Fireworks AI, Lightning AI, Railway, Warp and, on 30 October, Northflank, with attackers hunting stored credentials that grant AI access. Wiz traced two stolen enterprise keys, one used for about 1.7 million model calls in thirteen hours, likely over $100,000 of usage at list price.
items.why: Teams that keep model API keys on hosting, CI or developer platforms, bank engineering teams and vendors included, should rotate them, scope them and cap spending.

items.headline: AI spending jitters hit tech stocks after Alphabet's worst day on record
items.summary: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have outlined more than $740 billion of capital spending this year, and investors are now focusing on negative free cash flow and rising debt, TechCrunch reported on 30 October. Alphabet fell 12 percent on Thursday, its worst day on record, and the Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent on Friday, with Nvidia down 4 percent.
items.why: For banks buying cloud and AI capacity, providers' cash strain and debt load become inputs to vendor-risk reviews and multi-year commitments.

items.headline: Anthropic renames its Max plans and lifts Ultra's five-hour limit for verified accounts
items.summary: Anthropic said on 30 October that Max 5x is now called Max and Max 20x is now Ultra, with prices unchanged at $100 and $200 a month. Verified Ultra accounts lose the five-hour usage limit, starting with most existing subscribers, while weekly limits stay; its pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro usage a week with $200 of monthly API credits.
items.why: Heavy users running long agentic sessions can work through a day without hitting a session cap once their account is verified.
items.for_your_skills: For your skills: on Ultra, formerly Max 20x, long runs such as a Signal sweep or an RFP assembly no longer stop at a five-hour cap once the account is verified.

say_it_today: Euro area supervisors now count about 85 percent of their banks using generative AI, and this week's attacks, from Binance to the AI developer platforms, put the scrutiny on what surrounds the models: engineers' devices, API keys and patching speed.
